rationale: B wins because it is tighter and more disciplined about what the facts can actually carry. Its best line, "Going's new planner is a Premium-only perk — and most of its 2 million members can't touch it," turns the launch into a real consumer-value tension. A has strong material, but "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" is a profile pitch wearing borrowed clothes; the update gives a former name, not a reinvention story.
gaps_in_A: "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" overreaches. The supplied facts support a former name and a launch, not a founder-profile arc or "long reinvention."
"flight-deal newsletter" and "deal-detection engine" are not in the update. They may be true in the real world, but this judging exercise is not a vibes buffet.
"the prevailing model in AI travel tools is intent-first" is an outside market claim with no support in the supplied facts. Prove it or strip it.
"A tech business reporter covering SaaS subscription models" miscasts Going. This is a consumer travel membership/paywall story, not SaaS unless you have actual B2B software facts.
gaps_in_B: "the dominant industry narrative" and "wave of 'AI will plan and book your whole trip' announcements" are invented context from outside the update. The no-booking angle is good; the fake peg needs evidence.
"category-creation" is too grand for the facts. The update proves a product extension from alert to itinerary, not a new category.

The first two angles both lean on the link-out/no-booking tension. They are different enough to keep, but the overlap should be tightened so one owns category shift and the other owns the booking gap.
"most of its 2 million members can't touch it" is a sharp line, but it needs the paid-base number before a founder should put it in front of a skeptical reporter.
